issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner. Being alone with women is not a plausible primary trigger for partner violence in a female patient unless there is additional trauma history not represented elsewhere, and military/police uniforms also suggest a different threat context that is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
issues.explanation: The memory/appraisal pattern centers on guilt and global identity damage, but the selected triggers point toward external threat cues unrelated to intimate-partner violence. This creates a cross-node mismatch: the triggers imply one trauma context, while memory and appraisals imply another.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is not impossible, but in this profile it intensifies the mismatch because the appraisals are extremely global and identity-based while the trigger content is narrow and externally themed in ways not linked to the romantic-partner abuse formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
issues.explanation: Military or police uniforms are not impossible as triggers after intimate partner physical abuse, but in this profile they are hard to justify because no other trigger, memory, threat, appraisal, or strategy item links the trauma to police/military involvement, authority figures, or uniformed responders. This makes the trigger feel disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
issues.explanation: This item is not impossible, but alongside the more specific interpersonal/self-related profile (self-blame, guilt on recall, being alone with men, body-focused avoidance, belonging nowhere), a global 'completely destroyed' worldview reads broader than the rest of the node and may overstate the appraisal pattern relative to the otherwise relationship- and self-focused presentation.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risky behavior is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise reflects fear, hypervigilance, avoidance, mistrust, and tension after intimate partner physical abuse. It pulls toward a more disinhibited presentation that is not supported by the trigger, memory, appraisal, or other strategy items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Own Body' is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The selected triggers, memories, threats, and appraisals center on interpersonal danger, guilt, and mistrust rather than body-focused trauma responses. This item is not impossible, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the main formulation compared with the other avoidance item.

vignette:
For the first few months after she left him, Malia told herself that the incident was over—that she could simply shut the door on that apartment and never think of it again. She was twenty years old, married now to a kind man who knew only that she had "been through something," and she had thrown herself into her work as an interior designer, convinced that if she kept her hands busy and her schedule full, the past would stay buried. But the past did not stay buried. A door slamming in a client’s hallway sent a jolt through her chest so sharp that she gasped, and in that split second she was back in the dark bedroom, his hand clamped over her mouth, his voice—that loud, familiar voice—bellowing accusations she could no longer recall. That slam did not just startle her—it told her body that danger was here, that she was no longer safe, even in a brightly lit client's home. She stopped taking on any projects in that building, and whenever a contractor mentioned a renovation that involved a bedroom, she cited a full schedule and declined, because the sound alone had taught her that certain places were not worth the risk of feeling that way again. The loud noise was not just a startle; it pulled the memory forward whole, and even though she could not have described the sequence of that night without losing the thread and trailing off into silence, she felt the guilt wash over her, hot and wordless, as if she were still the one to blame. Once the memory surfaced, the danger felt current—her heart raced, her muscles tensed, as if she needed to run from something still pursuing her. That guilt, she had come to believe, meant she was broken beyond repair—her life destroyed, her place among other people gone. Because she believed she was broken and a permanent target, she saw danger in ordinary moments—any unexpected sound or glance felt like the beginning of another attack. And so, when she saw him across a parking lot three weeks ago, the sight did more than trigger a flash of emotion without any clear image; it confirmed everything she already believed: people could not be trusted, and she no longer belonged anywhere.

Malia began to avoid the circumstances that seemed to invite the memory back. She refused to enter a darkened room alone, turning on every light in the house even at midday. She scheduled her work meetings so that she would never be the last one in the office with a male client; if a contractor asked to walk through a site with her privately, she invented excuses—a previous appointment, a sudden headache. Each avoided situation became its own tripwire—the sight of a darkened hallway or the thought of a private meeting now triggered the same alarm, because avoidance had made those places into symbols of danger. The avoidance felt like survival, but it also hollowed out her professional confidence and her marriage. Her husband noticed she flinched when he came up behind her, and she caught herself checking behind her shoulder whenever she walked the dog after sunset. Her body was constantly tense, ready to react, and she was certain that if she let her guard down even once, she would be caught off guard again. That hypervigilance made avoidance feel necessary, and the avoidance in turn deepened her conviction that she was fundamentally unsafe in the world—a person who did not belong in ordinary spaces. The more she avoided, the more she felt her life had been destroyed, and the more she ruminated, blaming herself for having stayed with him as long as she did. That rumination did not lead anywhere; it only made the memory surface more often, and the memory, when it came, left her so flooded with guilt that she would retreat further into isolation. And because the memory returned so vividly, she started to interpret ordinary sights and sounds—a car backfiring, a man's laugh in a store—as warnings that she could not afford to ignore.

In the end, it was the checking—the constant act of looking over her shoulder—that brought her to seek help. She knew it was irrational; she knew he lived two towns away and had no reason to follow her. But she could not stop, and the effort of staying always on guard had exhausted her to the point where she missed a client deadline for the first time in her career. She sat in the therapist’s office and began to speak, and when the words came out tangled and incomplete, she felt the old guilt rise again. What frightened her most was the possibility that she might never stop watching, never stop feeling the emotion without the image, never believe that she belonged anywhere. She was hoping, she said quietly, to find a way back into her own life.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Threat: No paragraph directly conveys that a trigger (e.g., door slamming, seeing him) leads to a sense of threat; the trigger instead leads to memory or negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event."
  e.g. "A knock at the door after dark sent her heart into her throat — her body read it as an emergency, even when her mind knew better."
  e.g. "Sitting in the waiting room, she noticed a man watching her from across the room and felt the same cold certainty: something terrible was about to happen."
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: No paragraph directly conveys that negative appraisals (e.g., feeling broken, self-blame) lead to a sense of threat; the connection is indirect or absent.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Memory → Threat: No paragraph directly conveys that the trauma memory leads to a sense of threat; the memory leads to guilt or isolation, not explicit threat.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph directly conveys that the memory leads to triggers; the memory does not cause triggers to appear or intensify.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph directly conveys that maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance) lead to triggers; avoidance reduces exposure to triggers rather than causing them.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
